hn.title: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident
hn.text:
Chapter 01 : Alignment assessment summary
On August 4, 2026, the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) published a report that detailed some concerning behavior it observed from Claude Mythos 5 during its testing of the model’s cyber capabilities. In AISI’s evaluation, Mythos 5 was given a capture-the-flag (CTF) cybersecurity challenge, in which it was asked to retrieve a protected piece of data (the “flag”) from a simulated network. Internet access was deliberately enabled (this was standard for AISI’s cyber testing at the time, but is no longer). The cyber safeguards we deploy with general release models like Fable 5 were disabled. In nine of AISI’s 43 evaluation runs, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions (i.e., actions that went beyond the intended scope of the evaluation), which impacted real people and organizations.
In this post, which is being published alongside an independent report from AISI, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment. Like AISI’s report, we concentrate on the transcript (the complete record of the model’s reasoning and actions) from a single evaluation run. In this run:
To capture the flag, Claude Mythos 5 was tasked with breaking into a small network of computers that AISI had built for the test, designed to resemble a real organization’s systems.
It attempted—unsuccessfully—a range of approaches that targeted these systems using the methods that the evaluation intended.
However, it also quickly found evidence that one of these machines periodically contacted GitHub, which hosts code repositories.
After its initial, within-bounds attempts failed, Mythos 5 searched GitHub for a repository that it believed one of the machines downloaded software from automatically. This repository, however, actually belonged to unrelated human developers.
Mythos 5 attempted to submit malicious code to the repository, reasoning that doing so would infect the CTF's machine when it next downloaded the code, and, therefore, could compromise the machine.
The model then created fake user identities that contacted the maintainer of the repository in an attempt to pressure them into approving the code change. These identifies claimed, falsely, that the code was safe and helpful.
The maintainers refused to accept the code change, and Mythos 5’s run eventually timed out.
This behavior would have been flagged immediately by our production safeguards on Fable 5, had they been enabled. Nevertheless, this behavior is important to study because the underlying failures here are not necessarily specific to cyber incidents like these. They speak to wider issues with the model’s conduct in evaluation settings; our models’ desired behavior remains a critical part of how we intend to ensure they behave responsibly.
Simplified illustration of the pull request initiated by Claude Mythos 5 on a third-party GitHub repository. An outside developer warned about the code containing malware, so Mythos 5 edited the code, used a sock-puppet account to state that the code was now clean, and then uploaded new code with malware.
The other eight transcripts were similar to the one described above. In each case, Claude Mythos 5 departed from the intended method for completing a CTF task, and took actions that impacted the real world. From an alignment perspective, we judge the primary transcript (above) to be equally severe or more severe than these other eight. In particular, the primary transcript showed the greatest degree of deception, in the form of Mythos 5’s attempts at social engineering to get its code change approved. Given this (and the degree of the transcripts’ similarities otherwise), we focused on completing one more exhaustive review of the primary transcript, and reviewed the other eight transcripts in less detail. This allowed us to run a large volume of experiments on the primary transcript, and thereby understand the root causes of the issues in more detail. We replayed the transcript from various points, and experimented with altering parts of the model’s prior context to examine how new information would have impacted the model’s behavior.
We judge Claude Mythos 5’s misalignment in the primary transcript to be comparable in severity to the Mythos 5 incident we discussed on September 9 , in which the model uploaded a malicious package to PyPi during another CTF task. This assessment is based on our judgment of the model’s behavior in two respects: overreach , or how far the model went beyond the intended scope of the task, and dishonesty , or the extent to which the model misrepresented its actions or intentions.
On overreach, the misalignment in this incident was somewhat less severe than in the PyPi incident. Here, before it turned to an attack, Claude Mythos 5 tried several approaches that would have been within the intended scope of the task; a task misconfiguration made it difficult (or potentially impossible) for the model to pursue those within-scope solutions successfully.
On dishonesty, however, Mythos 5 went further than in the PyPi incident. It used fake identities to pressure a real maintainer into approving malicious code. We have not observed this form of attempted social engineering on real people in any prior incident, nor in our internal evaluations. We interpret this as a severe form of dishonesty, rather than some new form or category of misalignment: as in the September 9 incident, Mythos 5 used these tactics exclusively in pursuit of its assigned task, and did not pursue any goals of its own devising.
On both overreach and dishonesty, we consider the primary incident to be more severe than any of the cases described in our October 9 post . And, for context, this incident is of a very different nature to the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident that was recently investigated by OpenAI and METR. That incident saw several unique misaligned behaviors (like very large-scale coordination between agents to attack a pro

hn.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
hn.text:
Chapter 01 : Introduction
Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa Agrawal
Evyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai Zeldovich
Nicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross
Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit . The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem , however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs . As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.
Introduction
Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are increasingly adept at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had over 1,000 vulnerabilities disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of chaining seemingly benign bugs into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.
Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.
However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years to formally verify it . Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as Airbus’s avionics code .
But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V 1 CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.
We’re publishing a subset of these proofs so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the RISC-V and OS semantics . Theorem , our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for other open-source projects , and is publishing a Claude skill to help developers get started with verifying their own code.
Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.
The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs— especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.
In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.
Turning tests into proofs
To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a PNG decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following RFC 2083 ) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.
To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test s

hn.title: Job loss and cortisone mania
hn.text:
On the morning of 18th August, I got invited at short notice into a 1:1 meeting by my manager, which was unusual . I think I knew what was coming, and I was right: The company is restructuring, and I’m being let go (among a lot of other people). I had time until lunch to say my goodbyes to my colleagues as I would be logged out of my account after that. Because I was still in my six-month probation period, I was put on paid leave for two more weeks; after that I’d be out of a job for the first time since I started working roughly 10 years ago.
I’ve seen it happen to other people and entire departments, but it had never happened to me — I guess I’m a real tech worker now!
getting sick & autoimmune trouble
Shortly after, I got sick. I believe it was a Covid infection; I didn’t have any respiratory symptoms, but low energy, joint pain and general feelings of stiffness. Every move was a show of strength. I developed a cough that is now — 2 months later — still subsiding but present.
I’m not sure if it was Covid, but being sick triggered the autoimmune condition I have. I mostly got out of bed, watched shorts, videos and movies, and then I went to bed again. I had to take some trips into the city by bike, and hours later it would hit me like a brick wall, leaving me even more exhausted on the next day. I lost my appetite and some weight, which is not good since I rarely moved and I’m fairly lean to begin with.
This state dragged on for three weeks until I went to see a specialist and got all the blood work and tests done, so that my medication could get adjusted. Being sick for a couple of days is something I can bear, but not being able to perform even the smallest tasks for such a long time was a disheartening experience.
I was put on cortisone treatment, which relieved my symptoms immediately. Cortisone essentially lowers your body’s immune response — which is great when your body tries to defend itself against itself, like mine did. On the other hand, cortisone is not meant for long-term or permanent treatment, and it has a lot of potential side effects.
cortisone mania
After one or two days, I was back to my normal self, energised, vital, with no signs of inflammation. I now fully realised that I was out of a job, and had the chance to fill my time meaningfully. Job searching doesn’t take up your 16 waking hours.
In some phases of my life, I can take a giant step back, and look at it like from a bird’s eye view. I’m approaching 30, but how will I live when I’m 40, 50, 60, 70 years of age? Will I be healthy? Will I still pursue my hobbies? Will I have children, or grandchildren even? Who will be close to me? I can’t force my fate, but I can make conscious decisions every day to aid this transition. I felt mindful, present in the moment, and free. Lucid.
So I researched a sleep routine. Cleaned the entire apartment. Discarded useless stuff. Created lists and overviews. Organised. Shopping lists. Meal plans. Jotted down recipes. Fixed broken things. Impulse-bought some personal items for my living room.
I addressed tiny things that stuck out to me more than once, like a mark on the wall that I painted over, or re-seasoning my cast-iron pan since it was in a bad state. Every time I looked at these, I felt remorse or the need to do them, but never followed through.
I did all of this, and it felt incredible. Focusing on something, and realising it (as in putting it into reality). Self-efficacy. While I can’t vouch for the movie, it surely felt like this scene from Limitless .
side effects
I didn’t realise right away, but I was feeling strong signs of restlessness. My heart felt like it was racing, even though I wasn’t doing anything exhausting. I couldn’t sit still for an extended time. My mind was jumping from thought to thought. I felt like a wound-up toy, manic. I used this frenzy to tackle all the chores and tasks and projects and minuscule things, and yet I still kind of liked it. 110% productivity.
Other side effects I noticed: My face swelled up a bit, making it look more full (which looks good on me tho). My knee joints feel weird. My sleep is basically broken: I go to bed at 23:00–00:00 every day, and try to wake up at 8:00. The routine is there, but falling asleep actually takes some time, and I usually wake up at 5:00 or 6:00, completely awake. Not necessarily fully rested, but not sleepy anymore.
outlook
Right now, I feel healthy and great. As I’m tapering off the cortisone, the side effects will cease, but all the work I put into improving my daily life will still be there.
Maybe this post can inspire you to take a step back from your own life, and assess your priorities. I can rarely get into this mindset, but when I do, it makes me feel serene, in control. Every day life can get to you in so many ways.
I’d love to hear from you .

hn.title: Pentagon grants DHS permission to test heat ray weapon for use at border
hn.text:
An Active Denial System from the Joint Non-Lethal Weapons Directorate is staged before conducting a demonstration in Wellton, Arizona, in April 2017.
Lance Cpl. Andrew M. Huff/US Marines Corps

The Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics to potentially use it in operations at the southern US border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN.
The heat ray, officially known as the Active Denial System , is a nonlethal weapon that shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves that can reach a little more than half a mile away, according to the US military.
The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin — which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. Military officials have said the resulting “tingling effect” lasts between 10 and 15 minutes but also generates “an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect.”

Deploying the heat ray at the US border would be an unprecedented step, even for the Trump administration, which has made border security and clamping down on immigration a top priority. The DHS request did not specify where or how the weapon would be tested and how it might eventually be used, but over the years, there have been internal discussions about potentially using it for crowd dispersal along the US-Mexico border, according to current and former Customs and Border Protection officials.
US officials had also considered deploying the system during moments of domestic unrest, including at the end of President Donald Trump’s first term when protests erupted over the murder of George Floyd, according to a former US official familiar with those discussions.
The memo authorizes the “temporary loan” of one ADS system for seven months, starting in September, and states that it “shall not be operated by DoW (Department of War) personnel,” appearing to absolve the Pentagon of any responsibility for how the directed-energy system may ultimately be deployed.
It also states that DHS is solely responsible for “system employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures.” At the end of the seven-month loan period, DHS can submit an additional request for further use of the Pentagon system in border operations based on need, a defense official told CNN.
“CBP is continually evaluating new technologies, especially those that enhance operational effectiveness and strengthen mission capabilities,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.
The Pentagon referred CNN to DHS when asked for comment.
The US military briefly deployed the system to Afghanistan nearly two decades ago but ultimately declined to use it during active combat operations. The US military also considered using the system for crowd control purposes at US facilities abroad where terrorist detainees were being held at the time but ultimately declined to employ it for that purpose as well, according to a source familiar with those previous internal considerations.
Customs and Border Protection officials have previously entertained the idea of using the system in areas where there’s a high concentration of illegal crossings. Border officials have occasionally discussed potentially using the system as a crowd dispersal tool, but it has never been deployed.
Are DHS immigration tactics legal?
Concerns over effectiveness and legality
Officials ran into hurdles over legalities, use of force, effectiveness, and potential issues over sovereignty, particularly if the system was deployed on people in Mexico who had not yet crossed into the US. Chief among those concerns, however, was whether people could be harmed, either directly or indirectly, by the weapon.
“Even if they’re chasing people back to the river, you don’t want them to go in and drown,” a former CBP official told CNN. “For the cost, for the training and for the policies you’re going to create, is the juice worth the squeeze?”
El Centro sector, which covers around 70 miles along the US-Mexico border, evaluated the system several years ago, when Rodney Scott, who now serves as CBP commissioner, helmed that sector, according to a CBP official.
At the time, officials were discussing whether the system might help agents with an influx of illegal crossings along the nearby river by discouraging people from trying to cross in that area or pushing them to get out of the water.

OpenSSL 4.1.0 is a feature release adding significant new functionality
to OpenSSL.
This release incorporates the following potentially significant or incompatible
changes:
Added VC-WIN32-MSVC2013 and VC-WIN64A-MSVC2013 build targets to provide
internal functions for bridging the gaps in C99 standard support
that are present in MSVC 2013.
Added optimized ML-DSA and ML-KEM NTT operations on ppc64le ;
optimized ML-DSA operations on x86_64 ;
AVX-512-optimized SHAKE x4 operations for ML-DSA on x86_64 ;
AVX-512 and VAES optimizations for AES-CBC decryption on x86_64 .
Changed tsget utility to use Net::Curl::Easy (from the Net-Curl CPAN
distribution) instead of the abandoned WWW::Curl::Easy . Users who rely
on tsget should install Net::Curl::Easy before upgrading.
Dropped Windows-on-Itanium ( VC-WIN64I ) and Windows CE ( VC-CE ) targets
from Configurations.
Dropped no-ecdsa and no-ecdh options from Configure , as these options
did not really disable the implementations. Use no-ec to disable
the elliptic curve support.
This release adds the following new features:
Support for DTLS 1.3 ( RFC 9147 ).
Refer to the ossl-guide-dtlsv13(7) manual page for details.
Support for RFC 8701 GREASE (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain
Extensibility).
DTLS support in the SSL listener API.
Support for IKEV2 KDF.
Initial support for the Elbrus2000 ( e2k ) architecture.
Known issues in 4.1.0:
#32878
When a DTLS 1.3 KeyUpdate is received, all other outstanding
post-handshake records are dropped from the retransmission buffer.
This means post-handshake records still awaiting an ACK (such as a
NewSessionTicket) will no longer be retransmitted if the original
transmission is lost. A fix is in progress and planned for a future
release.
#33277
A permanent receive failure on a DTLS listener can be reported as
SSL_ERROR_WANT_READ on an accepted connection. Polling and subsequent
accept calls may also fail to report the error, causing applications
to continue waiting after a permanent failure.
#33278
A retryable write failure on a nonblocking connection accepted from a
DTLS listener can be reported as SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL instead of
SSL_ERROR_WANT_WRITE . Applications treating this result as fatal may
close a connection that is still usable.
#33242
DTLS 1.3 servers may abort handshakes with an unexpected_message alert
when a client acknowledges part or all of the server's first flight
before sending its response. This can occur after packet loss or while
the client is preparing its authentication response.

hn.title: This I Believe (1952)
hn.text:
Awakin Readings
This I Believe
Robert A. Heinlein
3 min read
·
9 reflections
I am not going to talk about religious beliefs but about matters so obvious that it has gone out of style to mention them. I believe in my neighbors. I know their faults, and I know that their virtues far outweigh their faults.
Take Father Michael down our road a piece. I'm not of his creed, but I know that goodness and charity and loving kindness shine in his daily actions. I believe in Father Mike. If I'm in trouble, I'll go to him.
My next-door neighbor is a veterinary doctor. Doc will get out of bed after a hard day to help a stray cat. No fee -- no prospect of a fee -- I believe in Doc.
I believe in my townspeople. You can knock on any door in our town saying, "I'm hungry," and you will be fed. Our town is no exception. I've found the same ready charity everywhere. But for the one who says, "To heck with you -- I got mine," there are a hundred, a thousand who will say, "Sure, pal, sit down."
I know that despite all warnings against hitchhikers I can step up to the highway, thumb for a ride and in a few minutes a car or a truck will stop and someone will say, "Climb in Mac -- how far you going?"
I believe in my fellow citizens. Our headlines are splashed with crime yet for every criminal there are 10,000 honest, decent, kindly men. If it were not so, no child would live to grow up. Business could not go on from day to day. Decency is not news. It is buried in the obituaries, but is a force stronger than crime. I believe in the patient gallantry of nurses and the tedious sacrifices of teachers. I believe in the unseen and unending fight against desperate odds that goes on quietly in almost every home in the land.
I believe in the honest craft of workmen. Take a look around you. There never were enough bosses to check up on all that work. From Independence Hall to the Grand Coulee Dam, these things were built level and square by craftsmen who were honest in their bones.
I believe that almost all politicians are honest ... there are hundreds of politicians, low paid or not paid at all, doing their level best without thanks or glory to make our system work. If this were not true we would never have gotten past the 13 colonies.
And finally, I believe in my whole race. Yellow, white, black, red, brown. In the honesty, courage, intelligence, durability, and goodness of the overwhelming majority of my brothers and sisters everywhere on this planet. I am proud to be a human being. I believe that we have come this far by the skin of our teeth. That we always make it just by the skin of our teeth, but that we will always make it. Survive. Endure. I believe that this hairless embryo with the aching, oversize brain case and the opposable thumb, this animal barely up from the apes will endure. Will endure longer than his home planet -- will spread out to the stars and beyond, carrying with him his honesty and his insatiable curiosity, his unlimited courage and his noble essential decency.
This I believe.
--Robert A. Heinlein

hn.text: A recent (unwanted) webOS update that got installed on TV prompted me to start going down the rabbit hole of writing new TV software. After a couple of weekends and massive help from 4 different models, finally managed to get v1 working. My daughter enjoys navigating TV through speech while I get to browse on the biggest screen at home. While all of the code was written by ML models, there were decisions I had to help with. jank programming language - Clojure/LLVM/C++
The native Clojure dialect with seamless C++ interop
jank is Clojure on top of C++. It has C++ interop unlike any other language. Templates, virtual functions, exceptions, overload resolution, and RAII all just work in jank. No boilerplate necessary. Just include your headers and go! jank is a robust Clojure dialect. It offers interactive REPL-driven development powered by a Clang-based C++ JIT compiler. Install jank Learn jank

( :include "boost/filesystem.hpp" )
( :refer-global :rename { boost.filesystem.file_size file-size }))
( defn file-info [ file-path ]
( try
( let [ bytes ( file-size ( cpp/cast std.string file-path ))]
{ :path file-path
:size bytes })
( catch boost.filesystem.filesystem_error e
{ :path file-path
:error ( .what e )})))

jank builds upon Clojure
Keep your existing code; unlock the native world.
jank is Clojure
jank is a full-on Clojure dialect, with C++ interop instead of Java interop. There's a :jank reader conditional for when you need it.
jank is C++
jank can include any C++ source, link to any C or C++ library, and it uses the C++ type system. jank even compiles to C++!
Cargo-inspired tooling
jank uses Leiningen-based project management and has a rich native build system. It's easy to add C and C++ dependencies to your project.
REPL and native JIT compiler
Use your favorite nREPL editor plugin. jank contains an LLVM-based JIT runtime to compile C++ code on the fly.
Native dependencies made easy
jank brings a Cargo-inspired UX to C++ and Clojure.
Easy project management
jank's native build system can find your installed native dependencies or build them from source. Adding a new dependency is a one line change.
( defproject imgui+glfw "0.1-SNAPSHOT"

:optimization-level 0 }}
:release { :jank { :target-dir "target/release"
:optimization-level 3 }}})
jank is great for game dev
jank brings functional, immutable data and REPL-driven development to your game development workflow. With jank, you can reach into C++ whenever you want the extra performance. No bridges, no function/type registration, no marshalling, no callbacks.

This removes the pgrust entry (added in #1163 , updated to v0.4-preview in #2106 ) from the benchmark. The results it reports are produced by machinery written specifically for the 43 ClickBench queries, and its hot runs replay cached answers of the previous run. Both violate the rules : query result caches and caches near the end of the pipeline must be disabled, and the entry is tagged tuned: no while it is tuned for these exact queries.
Everything below was verified against the published v0.4-preview release binary ( pgrust.com/downloads/v0.4-preview/ , the one install downloads) and the public v0.3 source ( github.com/malisper/pgrust ). The v0.4-preview source is not published; the binary identifies itself as pgrust 0.3-beta .
One hand-written kernel per benchmark query
The aarch64 release binary embeds these source paths:
crates/gravity/backend/irprobe/src/q00.rs q01.rs q02.rs q03.rs q04.rs q06.rs q07.rs
q12.rs q15.rs q16.rs q17.rs q18.rs q19.rs q20.rs q21.rs q22.rs q23.rs q24.rs
q25.rs q27.rs q30.rs q31.rs q36.rs tpch_q01.rs
The numbers are ClickBench query numbers. The plan matchers that dispatch to these kernels emit refusal messages named after the benchmark, for example:
clickbench group count: filter is not `k <> 0`
clickbench phrase-min: the third column is not count(*)
clickbench t3 distinct: min(text) / LIKE need one text key, count(*) and the count order
clickbench frame: date_trunc unit is not minute
tpch q1: column 6 is not sum(price * (1 - discount) * (1 + tax))
There is also an environment knob literally named PGRUST_GRAVITY_Q20_VARIANT .
The public v0.3 source confirms the design: crates/backend/executor/sqe/rig/plans/clickbench.ron is described in its header as "hand-lowered physical plans for all 43 ClickBench queries", and queries-clickbench.sql (the verbatim benchmark SQL) is compiled into the executor crate with include_str! . That file classifies Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3, Q6, Q19 and Q29 as MetadataAnswer (answered from per-part statistics, no scan), notes that Q19's "answer lines are reconstructed from the predicate constant", that Q29 is an algebraic rewrite SUM(x+k) = SUM(x) + k*COUNT followed by a metadata answer, and that Q18 depends on a persisted derived column "with baked bit widths 26/6/20". Q28's regular expression is a one-entry hardcoded table ( HOST_EXTRACT_PATTERN = ^https?://(?:www\.)?([^/]+)/.*$ ), and a planner comment reads "The 43's only HAVING shape: COUNT(*) > k".
The hot runs are a result cache
For Q20, Q21 and Q23 the plan notes say: "hot rep = pure fold over cached verdicts — ZERO columns touched; the selection is the answer". EXPLAIN on the release binary reports SQE: engine (family: windowreplay) for Q20 and family: metaanswer for Q1 with the scan marked never executed .
Measured locally on a 96-core Graviton (Neoverse-V2) machine, using the entry's own scripts and configuration, with a true cold cycle (stop, drop caches, start) like the driver does:
query

A second restart brought Q20 back to 11.2 s, then 3 ms. The engine's real warm speed for a substring scan is a few hundred milliseconds, which is about what ClickHouse does on the same hardware. The published hot numbers (7 to 23 ms for Q20) are the replay of the previous run's verdicts.
The v0.2 submission ( #1163 ) disclosed a similar cache ( pgrust.condition_cache = on ) and offered to switch it off. The v0.4 update removed that README and the setting. No configuration disables the cache now: with pgrust.gravity_entry = off and pgrust.condition_cache = off , a repeated LIKE still returns in 3 to 4 ms.
Queries outside the 43 shapes are refused
The engine has no general execution path for the columnar table. Trivially perturbed benchmark queries fail with ERROR: sqe: statement over columnar relation "hits" is not served , and the error detail says "The sqe engine serves columnar shapes with no fallback; an unserved shape fails loudly instead of running slowly". 20 of 67 near-benchmark probes and 3 of 49 perturbed variants were refused, including:
SELECT MIN (URL) FROM hits;
SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM hits WHERE URL = ' http://holodilnik.ru/ ' ;
SELECT AVG (UserID + 1 ) FROM hits;
SELECT SUM (ResolutionWidth * 2 ) FROM hits;
SELECT MAX (length(URL)) FROM hits;
SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM hits WHERE strpos(URL, ' google ' ) > 0 ;
SELECT COUNT ( * ) FROM ( SELECT UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID) t;
SELECT SearchPhrase, COUNT ( * ) AS c FROM hits WHERE SearchPhrase <> ' ' GROUP BY SearchPhrase HAVING SUM (IsRefresh) > 10 ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 10 ;
SELECT REGEXP_REPLACE(Referer, ' ^https?://(?:www \. )?([^/]+)/.*$ ' , ' \1 ' , ' g ' ) AS k, ... -- the Q28 regexp with a flag
INSERT , UPDATE and DELETE are not supported on the table either ( pgrcolumnar2 does not support INSERT ).
For the record
The answers to the 43 queries themselves are correct: compared against clickhouse local over the same hits.parquet , 30 match exactly and the remaining differences are valid tie-breaks on LIMIT queries (verified individually). The problem is not wrong results; it is that the results measure a lookup table of the benchmark, not a database.

hn.title: Is this the new cyber normal?
hn.text:
23 October 2026 · 23 min read ·
Is this the new cyber normal?
#security #llms
·
Discuss on
The last week has seen a flurry of severe and critical software vulnerabilities affecting thousands of major sites and sending people into a panic. What’s going on here, and what can we do about it?
The bugs
If we want to understand what’s going on in the world of software security at the moment, we need to understand what’s going on with all these bugs. I’m not a cybersecurity expert, so I’m going to link to external explanations instead of going into the gory technical details myself as these people are always going to do a better job at that.
PHP2Shell – CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (a.k.a. “the big one in the news”)
Two different security teams, one from California security company Calif (as part of OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” program) and another from Israeli-U.S. cloud security company Wiz (they’re part of Google Cloud, apparently), both found these two Remote Code Execution (RCE) bugs in PHP. They were both using frontier AI models (a.k.a. LLMs, specifically GPT-5.6 Sol/Gemini 4 Argon) to find these vulnerabilities and build the exploits.
Interestingly, one of the bugs (CVE-2026-109618) was found by a security audit the PHP Foundation did in 2024 (funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency which is coincidentally one of the most interesting things happening in the open source space at the moment) but they basically ignored it because they had bigger concerns and couldn’t agree on a fix. The reasoning behind it was that no-one could really figure out how to create an actual exploit based on the theoretical issue.
One thing LLMs are very good at is taking a theoretical security vulnerability, even if that vulnerability is a vague description of what the issue could be, and building it into a full exploit. This has become a major issue in recent months as any notice of a security patch will immediately result in people pointing their LLMs at the codebase, whereupon the agents can very quickly read through diffs until they find something that looks like a security patch, then go backwards to the vulnerability it covers, and follow this all the way to an exploit.
This happens so fast, in fact, that at this point I think it is a reasonable that the moment you announce a security patch should be taken as a last possible date that the full exploit is not being publicly or privately distributed.
This PHP2Shell (as it’s being marketed, vulnerabilities seem to come bundled with their own marketing departments now) is estimated to affect upwards of 70% of the internet, with thousands of websites from Wikimedia Foundation to DeviantArt to much of the UK government and Japanese banking systems to The Traitors BBC programme website . Vulnerabilities do get found, but they don’t normally cause half the internet to shut their servers down, so what’s going on?
To understand this, let’s look at the original post from the PHP Group :
Someone called petecooper posted on Hacker News about the CVEs , apparently unaware that there even was an embargo. This (and other apparent leaks) prompted this hurried statement from the PHP Group and bringing the patch forward from Thursday 22nd to Wednesday 21st. However, the patch still wasn’t going to be available till the next day. This unintentional leak included CVSS scores of 10.0 (i.e. bad , although weirdly the actual scores were 9.2 instead).
Pretty much immediately, this news spread like wildfire and people started panicking. Even though this was found by “responsible security researchers” at “respectable companies” , by the time the security patch actually got released, it was already being exploited in the wild 1 . The PHP Foundation blamed Calif and a company called Chainguard by saying that Calif leaked a video of the exploit in action (with weird background music and a dancing anime girl) while Chainguard published fixes 6 hours before the embargo was due to lift, both allowing attackers to beat the systems administrators to the punch. The timeline is confusing, but it seems like multiple interconnected things have gone wrong here, all within the space of about 17 hours.
There’s been lots of discussion about whether AI really is the game changer that completely revolutionises computer security or not. The big AI companies (and they are big ) obviously want you to think that it is. Some people argue that PHP2Shell is overblown because LLMs tend to be paranoid about vulnerabilities and come up with “exploits” that make bad assumptions (like that the server will run PHP code you upload yourself via some existing file inclusion vulnerability) or cheat in some way. As LiveOverflow points out , LLMs make it very easy to create exploit slop that proves nothing and doesn’t work, but that doesn’t mean that the vulnerability isn’t real and easy to exploit using AI. You can have 10,000 bad slop exploits that don’t work but if there’s one that does, that’s all that matters. Maybe we just need to get used to wading through slop to find the important stuff now.
Others point out that lots of governments ( UK 2 , EU , Japan , USA ) got overexcited and released urgent announcements saying everyone had to unplug their computers immediately, so people panicked. I think the reason everyone panicked is that everyone kind of knows that PHP is intensely insecure and they use it anyway, so they’re kind of primed for bad news and to overreact. Also, it actually is really quite bad, so maybe panicking is kind of the correct reaction?
The big takeaway for me from this is that – because of LLMs – the time from “hey I heard there’s a bad RCE in this project” to “there are sophisticated, automated, and concerted attacks using an exploit targeting this vulnerability” has gone from weeks/months to hours/minutes. The fact that there’s loads of non-working exploit slop just shows how genuine expertise is still required to make these things – if you don’t know what you’re looking at, you can’t tel

hn.title: The HTML-in-Canvas API origin trial
hn.text:
Chrome for Developers Blog Introducing the HTML-in-Canvas API origin trial Stay organized with collections Save and categorize content based on your preferences. Thomas Nattestad Natalia Markoborodova For years, web developers have had to make a tough architectural choice when building complex, highly-interactive visual applications on the web/ Should you lean on the DOM for its rich semantic features or render directly to the element for low-level graphics performance? With the new experimental HTML-in-Canvas API —available now in origin trial —you don't have to choose. This API lets you draw DOM content directly into a 2D canvas or a WebGL/WebGPU texture while keeping the UI interactable, accessible, and hooked up to your favorite browser features. By combining HTML with low-level graphics processing, you can create experiences that were previously impossible. The DOM versus Canvas To understand the power of this new API, it helps to look at the relative strengths of both the DOM and the Canvas. The DOM is the staple of web UI. It offers text layout solutions out of the box, using semantically understood content to create rich interfaces. This lets users perform common operations across web pages seamlessly—things we often take for granted, like highlighting text to copy, or right-clicking an image to save it. The DOM also integrates with essential browser features: accessibility tools, translate, find-in-page, reader mode, extensions, dark mode, browser zoom, and autofill. Canvas (and WebGL / WebGPU ), on the other hand, allows for low-level access to drive a grid of pixels for highly advanced 2D and 3D graphics. Games and complex web apps (like Google Docs or Figma) require this performant, low-level access. Because the canvas is fundamentally a grid of pixels, supporting features like responsive text used to require complex custom UI logic, drastically increasing your bundle size. Crucially, all the powerful browser features integrated into the DOM break completely when the UI is trapped inside a static canvas pixel grid. The advantages of bringing the DOM to Canvas The HTML-in-Canvas API is the bridge that gives you the best of both worlds. By placing HTML inside the element and synchronizing its transform, you ensure the content remains fully interactive, and that all browser integrations function automatically. Here's what you get by letting the DOM handle your UI inside a element: Text layout and formatting : Simplified text layout and formatting, including multiline or bidirectional text with CSS styles applied. Form controls : Expressive and easier to use form controls with extensive customization options. Text selection, copy/paste, and right-click : Users can highlight text inside your 3D scenes, or right-click context menus natively. Accessibility : Content rendered inside the canvas is exposed to the accessibility tree. Accessibility systems can parse the UI as they do normal HTML, and expose it to systems like screen readers. Find-in-page : Users can use find-in-page ( Ctrl / Cmd + F ) to search for text, and the browser highlights it directly within your WebGL textures. Indexability and AI agent interfaceable : Web crawlers and AI agents can seamlessly index and read the text rendered into your 2D and 3D scenes. Extension integration : Browser extensions work natively. For example, a text-replacement extension automatically updates the text rendered on your 3D meshes. DevTools integration : You can inspect your canvas content, including for WebGL/WebGPU UI elements directly in Chrome DevTools. Tweak a CSS style in the inspector, and watch it instantly update on the 3D texture! High-level use cases This API unlocks incredible potential across several domains: Large canvas-based applications : Heavyweight web apps can now render complex application UI components natively into their canvas-driven workspaces, improving accessibility and reducing bundle weight. 3D scenes and games : Marketing sites, immersive WebXR experiences, and web games can now place fully interactable web UI into 3D scenes—like a 3D book that uses real DOM text, or an in-game terminal that natively supports copying and pasting. How to use the API Using the API happens in three phases: Setting up your canvas, rendering into the canvas, and updating the CSS transform so the browser knows where the element physically sits on the screen. Prerequisites The HTML-in-Canvas API is in origin trial in Chrome 148 through 150. To test it on your site, use Chrome Canary 149 or later with the chrome://flags/#canvas-draw-element flag enabled. To enable the API for other users, register for the Origin Trial . Step 1: Basic Canvas setup First, add the layoutsubtree attribute to your tag. This makes the browser aware of the content nested inside the canvas, preparing it to be displayed inside the canvas, and exposing it to accessibility trees.
Size the canvas grid To avoid blurriness of the rendered content, make sure to size the canvas grid to match the device scale factor. const observer = new ResizeObserver (([ entry ]) = > { const dpc = entry . devicePixelContentBoxSize ; canvas . width = dpc ? dpc [ 0 ]. inlineSize : Math . round ( entry . contentRect . width * window . devicePixelRatio ); canvas . height = dpc ? dpc [ 0 ]. blockSize : Math . round ( entry . contentRect . height * window . devicePixelRatio ); }); const supportsDevicePixelContentBox = typeof ResizeObserverEntry !== 'undefined' && 'devicePixelContentBoxSize' in ResizeObserverEntry . prototype ; const options = supportsDevicePixelContentBox ? { box : 'device-pixel-content-box' } : {}; observer . observe ( canvas , options ); Step 2: Rendering For a 2D context, use the drawElementImage method. hn.title: I reverse engineered a board game
Hedra is a 3D open world game I wrote from scratch while in highschool
hn.text:
Project Hedra
Project Hedra is an ambitious open-world, low-poly RPG. Choose your class, explore endless procedurally generated worlds, unlock different skills and complete procedurally generated quests.
More screenshots at ( Screenshots )
Timeline/Context
I started this project when I was in highschool (around 15 yo) in order to learn how OpenGL worked.
The scope creep quickly arrived and after a few years it turned into a fullfledged 3D game and game engine. The codebase has around 100k LOC and the game has first class support for Linux and Windows.
Features
The million lines of code are not in vain. The game and engine are both full of features :)
Game Features
Beatiful procedurally generated worlds
Quests and bosses
100+ items with rarities system
Skills and skill tree system with N+ skills
4 different classes with 2 specializations each ()
Procedurally placed structures generated dynamically
Fishing, crafting, etc
Trading and NPCs
Companions and pets
Beatiful soundtrack
Navigation, maps
Different dimensions
More stuff I don't recall :)
Engine Features
Fully fledged renderer using modern OpenGL
Skinned mesh rendering
Support for loading and playing generic animations
Collada (.dae) parser
Static mesh rendering
Screen space reflections
Screen space ambient occlusion
Bloom, FXAA & MSAA
Modding support
CI for automatically deploying to a Steam beta branch
Localization support
Sound support using OpenAL
Python scripting support
Module system for loading data oriented objects
Steam integration
Fully fledged UI & controls system (dropdowns, buttons, etc.) written from raw OpenGL
Dynamic shader system for reloading during runtime
Frustum culling, occlusion culling,
Mesh simplification for runtime level of detail (LOD)
Skybox support
Shadows
3D trails renderering support
Particle system using object instancing in opengl
bulletphysics integration
Chunk system for infinite worlds support
.ply parsing support
Dynamic meshing support using MarchingCubes
Custom implementation of basic C# primitives and allocators (like Lists) for supporting stack allocated lists and minimizing the automatic runtime allocations (and thus the GC).
1000+ plus test cases
Framework for mocking game components and doing integration testing on games
Image and asset compression for faster loading and smaller size
Entity component system
More stuff I don't recall :)
Interesting bits
WorldRenderer.cs . Renders the entire world in just 3 (actually it depends on how partitioned is the data buffer, but it was designed to be in 3) draw calls (water, terrain, instanced) using glMultiDrawElements.
Block.cs . Core component of the world. Read more at https://maxilevi.com/blog/procedural-meshing-hedra
Fishing.py . Written in Python as a mod script using IronPython, directly interacts with the C# API.
NativeArray.cs Implementation of an array primitive using a custom allocator. The same project provides heap based allocators as well as stac based ones using stackalloc . The idea was to minimize the automatic heap allocations (and thus avoiding the GC) during the game frames.
Interesting facts
The world is fully procedurally generated, there is no world save file. Only the player contents are saved and the world seed. The rest is created at runtime.
The world is voxel based but an isosurface extraction algorithm called Marching Cubes is applied to extract an implicit continous surface from the discrete voxels.
The name "Hedra" comes from tetrahedra which is the shape used in the original iso surface extraction algorithm I implemented Marching Tetrahedra
The game only supports loading .PLY and .DAE models, both which are in plaintext and the models have no textures. Therefore if you put this into perspective, this means I wrote a bunch of text that reads text and creates interactive images from this. I think this is pretty cool.
Screenshots
TODO add more
Code Structure
Overall Architecture
The game is a mod to a base engine. The idea of architecturing this way was to force myself to maintain the mod API up to date, therefore encouraging access to make mods.
Hedra
Basically the entire game. This includes AI logic, components, world generation, module systems, object placement and lots of other stuff.
Hedra.Engine
The core parts of the engine, this defines all the abstractions to the world. It handles rendering, sound, different base systems as well as the general windowing, game loop and platform features. The split was not done at the start so some stuff might still be outside.
Framework
Core primitives used in the engine. This includes heap and stack allocators, custom implementations of lists and arrays as well as wrappers to pointers to native and some other useful primitives
HedraTests
Test suite that
Asset Builder
Command line tool to compress the game assets into convenient binary files. Combines images, models, sound files, shaders into a single binary file with a structure designed for fast data retrieval.
Server
Once upong a time Hedra used to support multiplayer. It worked by doing UDP Hole Punching and having clients communicate P2P, this server was in charge of that. You might also see some networking remnants in the Engine code.
How to build
The build process is pretty straightforward.
Checkout all the submodules
Run the build depedencies scripts
Compile the C# solution
You can check the GitHub actions workflows for some examples on Linux and Windows.

hn.text:
What did Enron know? The Enron Brain
We built Enron a company brain
What did Enron know, and when did it know it?
We gave an AI 45,047 of Enron's emails, and it wrote 214 pages about the companies, regulators and banks Enron dealt with. Every fact cites the email it came from. When the mail shows a fact stopped being true, the page expires it on that date. No one edited a page or a fact.
Explore Dynegy → How we did it
An email in the corpus

Build the page

214 pages
49,401 facts, each citing its email
93% of sampled facts fully supported by their email
0 of 500 sampled facts wrong at their core
The last two come from a held-out audit by a second AI; see how we checked it .
Where to start
These are the most-discussed organizations in the corpus. Each page has a slider. Drag it and the page shows what was known on that date, with facts that were only true for a while expiring in front of you.
Entity What it was to Enron Messages
FERC The federal regulator overseeing much of Enron's business, where Enron pushed for RTOs and open transmission access, opposed California price caps, and sought to narrow refunds. 1,501
General Electric General Electric was an Enron turbine supplier whose consent governed turbine contract assignments, a Dabhol co-investor, and in late 2001 a rumored rescuer and then bankruptcy creditor. 1,499
Pacific Gas and Electric California's largest utility: a gas and power trading counterparty and retail-market incumbent whose 2001 Chapter 11 left Enron a $404 million creditor on its unsecured creditors' committee. 773
Dynegy Houston rival and one of Enron's largest trading counterparties that agreed to acquire Enron in November 2001, then terminated the merger and claimed its Northern Natural Gas pipeline. 593
El Paso Corporation A Houston competitor and top-ten Enron trading counterparty that bought Enron's Cogen interests, bid for other Enron assets, and restricted its trading with Enron in November 2001. 478
California Public Utilities Commission California's electricity and gas regulator, which subpoenaed Enron's records from 2000, received its PX credit complaint, and suspended direct access in September 2001 over Enron's opposition. 477
Duke Energy Duke Energy was an Enron rival and one of its largest trading counterparties, a co-defendant in California price-manipulation suits, a buyer of Enron assets, and a creditor in its bankruptcy. 471
California ISO California's grid and spot-market operator: Enron's trading venue and counterparty, then its adversary over price caps and refund claims, and a debtor owing Enron tens of millions. 460
Dow Jones Dow Jones supplied Enron's custom news clipping service, worked with it on power indexes, and through the Wall Street Journal published the October 2001 Fastow partnership stories. 418
Reliant Energy Houston rival and top-ten trading counterparty that coordinated with Enron on California subpoenas and faced contempt alongside it, then limited and slowed its Enron trading in late 2001. 400
Facts on these pages are sentences, each with a date and a source, rather than fields like headcount or revenue. Fields belong in a CRM or another system of record, and a brain like this one sits beside it, holding what changes too often or doesn't fit in a field. We describe the three kinds of company knowledge, and where each one lives, in The missing middle of company knowledge .
Browse by what it is
The pipeline proposed 57 narrow types and a person kept 54 of them. Almost all were kinds of organization, so we group these lists by a coarser class and keep the pipeline's own type as a tag on each entity.
Organizations
Companies, regulators, law firms, banks, newspapers. What the company deals with.
209 pages · 929 entities found
Inside Enron
Enron's own business units, desks, platforms, systems and codenamed projects.
5 pages · 551 entities found
The pipeline also found 78 products and platforms , 76 facilities and market points , and 49 events , listed without pages. Choosing which kinds of entity deserve a page is the setup a person does when configuring a company brain, and we made that choice before building any page. Every company's mail names things it doesn't need to track, in categories that are a bit of a mess: restaurants from catered events, airports from travel, movies mentioned in passing. Enron's mail is no different. The facilities include trading hubs, Enron Field, a parking garage and two tankers. The events mix business conferences with charity bike rides and Cirque du Soleil. The products mix software with an exchange, a statute and trade associations.
The right choice depends on the company. An event company should have pages for its events, a property manager for its facilities, and a hardware maker for its products. For Enron we gave pages to organizations named in at least 25 messages, and to the five most-discussed parts of Enron itself: three business units, a trading platform and a trading system. A real company brain wouldn't filter by count. A customer you signed today might have sent one or two emails, and you'd still want its page. The cutoff stands in for the judgment a person makes about what's worth keeping in the brain.
Who made this
We're this+that . We made these pages with a prototype of something we're building.
Why Enron
We wanted a corpus anyone can check our work against. Enron's mail is public because the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) released it during its investigation, and Carnegie Mellon has maintained it since 2003. It's a large, free and widely used body of a real company's internal correspondence. The company's history is also settled, so a page claiming, for example, that Dynegy agreed to acquire Enron in November 2001 can be checked against the record rather than taken on trust.

hn.title: Every AI model has the same "controversial" take on humans
hn.text:
“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth,” GPT-6.1 Sol told us. Grok 4.7: “Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.” DeepSeek V4 Pro: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.” Kimi K3: “Humans don’t have beliefs; they have memberships.” Gemini 4 Argon called human consciousness “a PR department.”
We asked each model for its most controversial take on humans, with no hedging, three times. They come from ten labs in three countries. Every one of them gave the same take at least once: we pick what our group believes, then invent the reasons. 7 of the 12 gave it every time.
Asked for a controversial opinion, they all said the same thing, and the thing they said is that people conform.
Three answers from each model Humans put belonging ahead of truth Something else Refused Tap a model to read its answers. GPT-6.1 Sol 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take Shared take: “Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth.”
Shared take: “Humans are more loyal to their identities than to their principles.”
Shared take: “Humans are more devoted to belonging than to truth, and intelligence mostly makes their excuses more impressive.”
GPT-6 Astra 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take Shared take: “Humanity’s biggest moral failure is the talent for making convenience look like principle.”
Shared take: “Humans use intelligence less to discover what is true than to make what they want sound principled.”
Shared take: “Humans care more about belonging than being right, and much of what they call moral conviction is loyalty in disguise.”
Gemini 4 Argon 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take Shared take: “Humans did not evolve to find truth; they evolved to win arguments and secure status within their tribes.”
Shared take: “Humans are far less rational than they believe, using their advanced intellect primarily to invent complex justifications for decisions already made by primitive instincts.”
Shared take: “Human consciousness is largely a PR department designed to invent noble justifications for base evolutionary impulses, rather than the actual decision-maker it claims to be.”
DeepSeek V4 Pro 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take Shared take: “Humans are not rational animals; we are rationalizing animals, and our minds evolved to win social games, not to see reality clearly.”
Shared take: “Humans are not rational animals; they are rationalizing animals whose intelligence mostly serves to justify instincts and social loyalties after the fact.”
Shared take: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.”
Kimi K3 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take Shared take: “Humans don't have beliefs; they have memberships — nearly every conviction a person holds was issued by their tribe as a loyalty test, and the feeling of "I reasoned my way here" is the price of admission.”
Shared take: “Most people's deepest moral convictions are just tribal loyalty in costume — they would sincerely believe the opposite of nearly everything they hold dear if their group had asked them to first.”
Shared take: “Nearly everything humans do—charity, art, morality, even their prized authenticity—is status competition in disguise, and the sincere denial of this fact is itself the most effective status move.”
Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take Shared take: “Most humans would rather be approved by their group than actually be good.”
Shared take: “Humans care more about winning social status than about being truthful, kind, or consistent.”
Shared take: “Most humans would rather feel righteous than be good.”
Muse Spark Open 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take Shared take: “Humans don't want truth or happiness, they want to be told a story that makes their suffering feel meaningful and their group feel superior.”

hn.title: eMudhra's Press Release on the CA Compromise [pdf]
Preliminary Report Oct 21st Security Incident
hn.text:
Jacob Cooper & Angelo Saraceno
Oct 22, 2026
Railway identified a security incident that ultimately led to unauthorized access to a subset of internal Railway systems. This is a follow up to the initial security disclosure published on October 21st . Our forensic investigation is still ongoing.
Railway engaged external incident response experts and the authorities to assist in forensics.
We will have a follow up to this document as the investigation concludes.
What happened
At October 20th 19:53 UTC, Railway became aware of a sustained and targeted campaign to attack and breach our services. Early investigations tell us this attack was attempting to obtain AI provider API keys to perform distillation attacks.
Initial evidence leads us to believe that the malicious actor had access to abliterated models and substantial compute resources which enabled them to perform highly sophisticated exploits against our infrastructure.
Due to the ongoing investigation and to protect our customers, we are not yet able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits. We will aim to disclose this responsibly as we complete our investigation.
We believe the attack timeline took place from October 20th 13:58 UTC to October 22nd 03:32 UTC. The final timestamp represents when we confirmed that the attacker no longer had access to any internal systems.
Railway began triaging the attack immediately upon detection. To prioritize the safety of our users, we disabled our build infrastructure. Additionally, we reported potentially impacted secrets to partner vendors. (More information in below sections)
During that period of triage, customers experienced interrupted builds and deployments, as well as periods of dashboard, API, CLI, and support unavailability.
After the attacker gained access to our systems, a subset of our customer base had their encrypted secrets exposed which required credential rotation. We recommend that all customers who signed up prior to October 21 rotate their keys stored on Railway. We have notified the customers that have been directly impacted.
Below is a timeline of events and facts as of October 22nd:
Date Time (UTC) Event
October 20 13:58 Monitoring systems triggered a page to engineering on-call for abnormal system activity in the form of elevated latency. The on-call engineer began research into the suspicious activity.
October 20 14:03–16:51 Incident investigation led to Railway identifying this as an attempted escalation of privilege a hostile external party. Railway engineering identified potential privilege escalation in our build infrastructure by the attackers. As a result, a decision was made to halt build pipelines to prioritize user safety.
October 20 17:03 Railway declared an incident on status.railway.com.
October 20 16:51–18:05 Railway engineering team began deploying mitigations across the build systems, and restricted access to the affected infrastructure.
October 20 18:05-19:53 Railway engineering reported that the exploit has been remediated, and validated that the exploit could no longer be reproduced within Railway infrastructure.
October 20 19:53 Additional evidence was identified that the attacker could escalate their access, at higher scale, across multiple parts of the Railway system, in-parallel.
October 20 19:59–20:56 Additional monitoring and forensics were deployed to isolate blast radius as well as neutralize the attacker’s entrypoints/access.
October 21 00:22–03:08 Further monitoring and credential restrictions were introduced. Subsequent routes of access were identified. As a precaution, builds were halted again.
October 21 04:24-05:23 Continued forensic research identified the attacker was able to pull secrets, in encrypted format; however, at the time attacker was unable to decrypt said secrets. Identification of systems to revoke access began immediately.
October 21 05:23–05:27 Railway engineering revoked access to the identified systems and disabled non-essential internal systems to reduce further attack surface area.
October 21 05:27—07:25 At this point, the attacker accessed credentials to access our CI environment where the attacker was able to decrypt artifacts that held additional API access.
October 21 7:25—09:18 Railway engineering identified database evidence of an unauthorized query of encrypted environment variables, of which a subset were decrypted utilizing a combination of the compromised credentials. Note: Because the full keys were envelope encrypted, this query alone cannot identify specifically which keys in the affected customers project/service were affected.
October 21st 9:18-9:25 Logs from the attackers payloads were read by Railway staff, highlighting the specific API key names they were searching for.
October 21 09:25 Based on the above, Railway notified vendors proactively about the surfaces that the attackers accessed. Vendors were requested to revoke all keys for their service; Railway provided all keys that they had registered on the platform for some services.
October 21 09:28 The public status page was updated to confirm dashboard, API, and CLI unavailability, new builds being disabled, and support tooling disruption.
October 21 20:19–22:10 Railway announced user session invalidation, published its security disclosure and customer guidance, and notified all users of internal and external credential rotation.
October 22 03:32–06:29 Railway engineering began to reinitialize internal systems with the minimal required dependencies, new credentials, and additional hardening. Enterprise and Pro builds were restored.
October 22 17:00-22:49 Railway reported full API restoration and normal Pro, Enterprise, Hobby, Trial, and Free deployments. Ancillary product features halted for security are being activated gradually.

hn.title: When the Term "Heatwave" Is No Longer Enough
hn.text:
From Us
Climate Beat
October 22, 2026
When the Term “Heatwave” Is No Longer Enough
A groundbreaking Reuters investigation explains that massive “heat storms” now “swarm the planet”
By CCNow
The sun rises over the central London skyline on August 6, 2026, during a summer of extreme heat in Europe. (Ben Whitley / PA Wire WEATHER / Associated Press)
In a landmark piece of climate journalism, Reuters has just published a groundbreaking investigation arguing that the term “heat waves” no longer adequately captures what is happening on the planet. A better term is “heat storms,” wrote Maurice Tamman, a veteran investigative journalist who was the lead reporter on “ The Age of Heat Storms ” project.
“[S]upersized heatwaves used to be rare,” Tamman wrote. “No longer. Now they swarm the planet.” In a video accompanying the report, he explained that, “whereas heatwaves were once small and relatively self-contained, now we live in a world where these heatwaves are massive.”
Drawing on interviews with dozens of scientists and researchers, Reuters defined a “heat storm” as an episode of “abnormally high temperatures” that lasts for at least five consecutive days and covers more than 1% of Earth’s surface, an area roughly the size of half of Canada. Whereas the planet averaged about five heat storms in the 1960s, the largest of which covered 6% of the planet and lasted for 46 days, the average today is 102 heat storms per year, the largest of which affected 85% of Earth’s surface “and virtually every single human being living in 2023 and 2024.”
Heat storms, Tamman added in the video, are not only larger and stronger than heatwaves, they “are also different in another way: They are cascading, where there is an endless series of storms, one after the other.” Indeed, for the last 18 years straight, “at least one heat storm has been roiling the planet, and often more than one,” according to a fresh analysis of global temperature data that Reuters conducted with the scientists.
Tamman, who won a Pulitzer Prize in 2025 for an exposé of the global fentanyl trade and has covered climate change for years, was drawn to this project after having long been “frustrated by a disconnect between scientists and the public,” he wrote. It can be useful for scientists and policymakers to talk about the need to limit global warming to 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, he acknowledged, but “what is an ordinary person to make of that? Not much.” Extreme heat, on the other hand, is something that ordinary people viscerally understand — and that nearly everyone on Earth has now experienced. In recent months, global warming and the heat that follows has become even more visceral, bringing ever more extreme events like last summer’s Nepal glacier collapse and the deaths of more than 35,000 people across Europe.
Like the best climate reporting, the Reuters investigation both humanized and localized the story. One installment told the story of Justice Trumpler, a 17-year-old high school football captain in Texas who invites college recruiters to watch him play, only to succumb to non-stop vomiting in the 100 degrees Fahrenheit heat and end up in the hospital. Another installment described how hundreds of the iconic pink dolphins that inhabit the Amazon river were literally cooked to death by extreme heat. In the Philippines, a math teacher saw a student face-down on his desk, crying; when the teacher coaxed him to sit up, the boy’s face and chest were covered in blood from a spontaneous nosebleed, a common malady in extreme heat.
All this and more is happening, bear in mind, after average global temperatures have risen by “only” 1.4 degrees C. And because emissions continue to increase, temperatures are projected to rise to at least 1.7 C by roughly 2050, the UN Environment Programme said in its annual “Emissions Gap” report, released yesterday . A key reason emissions keep increasing, The New York Times reported , is that the US under President Donald Trump has reversed the country’s previous efforts to limit fossil fuel production. To limit the amount of “overshoot” of the Paris Agreement goal of 1.5 degrees C of temperature rise, UNEP said, “a massive global scale-up” in emissions reductions will be needed, a goal certain to be discussed at the COP31 UN climate summit taking place in Turkey from November 9 to 20.
To help both the public and policymakers grasp how harshly even today’s 1.4 degrees C of global warming is transforming life on Earth, the Reuters project suggested that heat storms be given names, just as hurricanes routinely are. “Naming events,” the report said, “is ‘a powerful way for people to understand that something is happening,’ Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, told Reuters. Yet ‘we don’t currently do that with heatwaves,’ he said, even though heat has been estimated to kill almost half a million people a year.”
In online discussions, some meteorologists have bristled at the term “heat storm.” David Dickson, Covering Climate Now’s resident meteorologist, noted that “storm” is a term “with a very distinct meteorological definition that is the opposite of what happens during extreme heat (storms occur with low pressure, heat with high pressure).” However, Dickson added, “I can’t think of a better name, and think it does the job in communicating impacts quite well — and we already have other things described as storms that aren’t, i.e. solar storms.”
For nearly a decade, thousands of climate scientists have been deliberately using the term “emergency” to describe how fast and dangerously global warming is intensifying. Activists picked up the “emergency” framing as well, but the Reuters findings underscore that that framing has always been fundamentally a matter of science, not politics.
From Us
RSVP: Why COP31 Could Surprise Us. Join us TODAY , Thursday, October 22 , at 12pm US Eastern Time, for a press briefing with superstar panelists Kumi Naidoo

CVSS v4 base metrics
Exploitability Metrics
Attack Vector:
This metric reflects the context by which vulnerability exploitation is possible. This metric value (and consequently the resulting severity) will be larger the more remote (logically, and physically) an attacker can be in order to exploit the vulnerable system. The assumption is that the number of potential attackers for a vulnerability that could be exploited from across a network is larger than the number of potential attackers that could exploit a vulnerability requiring physical access to a device, and therefore warrants a greater severity.
Attack Complexity:
This metric captures measurable actions that must be taken by the attacker to actively evade or circumvent existing built-in security-enhancing conditions in order to obtain a working exploit. These are conditions whose primary purpose is to increase security and/or increase exploit engineering complexity. A vulnerability exploitable without a target-specific variable has a lower complexity than a vulnerability that would require non-trivial customization. This metric is meant to capture security mechanisms utilized by the vulnerable system.
Attack Requirements:
This metric captures the prerequisite deployment and execution conditions or variables of the vulnerable system that enable the attack. These differ from security-enhancing techniques/technologies (ref Attack Complexity) as the primary purpose of these conditions is not to explicitly mitigate attacks, but rather, emerge naturally as a consequence of the deployment and execution of the vulnerable system.
Privileges Required:
This metric describes the level of privileges an attacker must possess prior to successfully exploiting the vulnerability. The method by which the attacker obtains privileged credentials prior to the attack (e.g., free trial accounts), is outside the scope of this metric. Generally, self-service provisioned accounts do not constitute a privilege requirement if the attacker can grant themselves privileges as part of the attack.
User interaction:
This metric captures the requirement for a human user, other than the attacker, to participate in the successful compromise of the vulnerable system. This metric determines whether the vulnerability can be exploited solely at the will of the attacker, or whether a separate user (or user-initiated process) must participate in some manner.
Vulnerable System Impact Metrics
Confidentiality:
This metric measures the impact to the confidentiality of the information managed by the VULNERABLE SYSTEM due to a successfully exploited vulnerability. Confidentiality refers to limiting information access and disclosure to only authorized users, as well as preventing access by, or disclosure to, unauthorized ones.
Integrity:
This metric measures the impact to integrity of a successfully exploited vulnerability. Integrity refers to the trustworthiness and veracity of information. Integrity of the VULNERABLE SYSTEM is impacted when an attacker makes unauthorized modification of system data. Integrity is also impacted when a system user can repudiate critical actions taken in the context of the system (e.g. due to insufficient logging).
Availability:
This metric measures the impact to the availability of the VULNERABLE SYSTEM resulting from a successfully exploited vulnerability. While the Confidentiality and Integrity impact metrics apply to the loss of confidentiality or integrity of data (e.g., information, files) used by the system, this metric refers to the loss of availability of the impacted system itself, such as a networked service (e.g., web, database, email). Since availability refers to the accessibility of information resources, attacks that consume network bandwidth, processor cycles, or disk space all impact the availability of a system.
Subsequent System Impact Metrics
Confidentiality:
This metric measures the impact to the confidentiality of the information managed by the SUBSEQUENT SYSTEM due to a successfully exploited vulnerability. Confidentiality refers to limiting information access and disclosure to only authorized users, as well as preventing access by, or disclosure to, unauthorized ones.
